primary_sources: Lyndon B. Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, May 22, 1964 (Public Papers of the Presidents)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, May 22, 1964

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Johnson's University of Michigan address, May 22, 1964; quotations are from the Public Papers of the Presidents.
stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of President Lyndon Johnson's commencement address at the University of Michigan, May 22, 1964. Johnson said, "The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning."

He named three places to begin building it: "in our cities, in our countryside, and in our classrooms."

parts.prompt: Identify one goal of the Great Society stated in the passage.
parts.modelAnswer: Johnson says the Great Society demands an end to poverty, so ending poverty is one goal stated in the passage. He pairs it with an end to racial injustice.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for identifying one goal from the passage, such as ending poverty or ending racial injustice.
scoring.notEarned: Naming a goal that is not in the passage, such as winning a war, does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Explain one reason Johnson believed the federal government could end poverty in the 1960s.
parts.modelAnswer: The postwar economy had grown fast, so Johnson believed the nation's abundance gave the government the wealth to act. He trusted that federal programs could fix social problems, as the New Deal had done in the 1930s.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one reason for Johnson's confidence, such as postwar abundance and growth, faith in activist government, or the example of the New Deal.
scoring.notEarned: Restating that Johnson wanted to end poverty, without a reason he believed it possible, does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Explain one way the Great Society changed the role of the federal government.
parts.modelAnswer: The Great Society put the federal government into new areas of daily life, such as health care for older Americans through Medicare. Washington took on duties that states and private charities had handled before.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one change in the federal role, such as federal health insurance, federal aid to poor schools, federal housing programs, or the Office of Economic Opportunity.
scoring.notEarned: Naming a program without saying how it changed the federal role does not earn the point.
